title: Flight fare quotes and seat holds
name: Fare quote service

questions.prompt: Is there a defect in how this code handles state shared between concurrent requests? If so, mark the line(s) where it is; otherwise answer that there is none.
FareQuoter is registered as a singleton but resolves IFlightInventory through IServiceScopeFactory inside QuoteAsync instead of taking it in the constructor. Why?
choices: So the quoter can cache inventory instances between requests for speed.
Because minimal API endpoints cannot resolve scoped services directly.
IFlightInventory is scoped; a singleton cannot receive a scoped service in its constructor, so the quoter creates a short-lived scope per call and the inventory lives only for that call.
To give each caller a private copy of the HttpClient and avoid sharing it between threads.

questions.prompt: Two POST /holds requests arrive at the same moment for 2 seats each on a flight with 3 seats remaining in the database. Both read remaining = 3 before calling TryHold. What happens?
choices: Exactly one succeeds and the other gets 409, because the check against the held count and the increment happen together under one lock.
Both succeed, because each request read remaining = 3 from the database before reaching the registry.
Both succeed unless the database row is locked by the inventory query.
Exactly one succeeds, but which one is decided by the database rather than the registry.

questions.prompt: RequestAudit is registered as scoped and holds a List<string>. Two requests run concurrently and each calls Record once. What does each request's log line report as its entry count?
choices: The second request logs 'entry 2' because both share the same list.
The list can be corrupted because it is accessed from two threads without a lock.
Both log 'entry 1' only if the singleton FareQuoter resets the list.
Both log 'entry 1': each request gets its own RequestAudit instance and list, so no cross-request sharing or locking is involved.
